chapter: Leaving Duke and the Hollywood years
title: Earning more after Duke, and the raise he won in 1930
summary: He made more money after leaving Duke and most with Louie, whose overhead was smaller, while Duke and Irving Mills kept the money and refused raises; he once quit in New York to get one.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Did you make more money with Freddie Slack than you did with Duke?

Oh, yeah. I made more money after I left Duke than I did with Duke, period. And I made more money than both of them when I went with Louie. Duke couldn't pay me the salary that Louie paid me, or he wouldn't and I wouldn't
Well, Louie made more money than Duke, though, too. Joe Glaser got him bookings where --
Yeah, and not only that. Louie's overhead wasn't as big as Duke's, you know.
Didn't have a big band move around. But And was never noted for his high salaries either. Duke would have a (unintelligible) out immediately.

Uh-huh. Well, Louie -- I mean, they made so much money with Louie that they couldn't take it out of the country, one country, to -- No kidding. They would buy skates or anything and sell them over there and made so much money.
But Louie wouldn't -- I mean, Duke wouldn't give a guy a raise if he wanted one. "Where am I going to get it. I ain't making no money." Him and Irving Mills got all the money, you know.
I quit him once. I quit him in New York. I got the raise. [Duke]
Oh, I can't think offhand. Around -- just before we went to Europe, I think. '31 or '30, something like that.
